survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD/PISA design document describes the assessment framework rather than an empirical analysis with an analytic dataset. It specifies that PISA is administered to 15-year-olds in schools using pencil-and-paper tests with a total testing time of about 2 hours per student, while the total item pool corresponds to about 7 hours across different student booklets. The document also describes background questionnaires for students and principals, but it does not provide any sampling-weight variable names or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife) for use in estimation. Because no microdata analysis is conducted here, complex survey weights are not applicable to the extraction; however, for any future empirical PISA analysis, analysts should use the official PISA sampling weights and replicate weights provided in the PISA database to account for the multistage school/student sampling design and booklet assignment.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is a framework and assessment-design description, not an empirical study that estimates achievement scores from student responses using PVs. While PISA achievement reporting is discussed conceptually (e.g., scales and calibration), the text does not specify any PV generation or combining procedure, nor any missing-data handling strategy for an analytic sample. Therefore, plausible values and missing-data handling are not reported because there is no model-estimation workflow evaluated in this publication.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: This publication does not define an analytic subsample for an empirical model. It describes the intended PISA 2000 administration: pencil-and-paper tests administered to 15-year-olds enrolled in school-based and work-based educational programmes, with each student taking about 2 hours of test time drawn from a larger item pool (about 7 hours worth of items across booklets). It also specifies that students complete a background questionnaire (20–30 minutes) and that school principals complete a questionnaire (about 30 minutes). No additional inclusion/exclusion criteria (e.g., grade restrictions, task completion thresholds, or missing-data exclusions) are specified because no dataset is analyzed in this document.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD/PISA 2000 design document explains how student knowledge and skills are measured across three domains: reading literacy, mathematical literacy, and scientific literacy, with each cycle focusing in depth on a “major” domain (reading in 2000, mathematics in 2003, science in 2006). It specifies pencil-and-paper administration with about 2 hours of testing per student, while the total item pool is much larger and is distributed across different booklets so that different students take different combinations of items. Achievement is reported on scales calibrated from the tasks, and the framework emphasizes functional, cross-curricular competencies rather than curriculum coverage alone. Contextual indicators are supported by student and school questionnaires, including a self-regulated learning instrument explored for the first cycle. The publication is not an empirical ML study and therefore does not report predictive performance metrics or model-based effects.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a framework/assessment-design publication describing the conceptual and operational structure of PISA (domains, task characteristics, questionnaires, and reporting scales) rather than conducting an empirical analysis on PISA microdata. As a result, there is no analytic sample size, no PV estimation procedure, no missing-data strategy for an evaluated dataset, and no ML model training or performance metrics to extract. The sparse ML-related fields are therefore expected by design.
